Vignette: Valentina, Age 27

Valentina grew up in a mid-sized city in Colombia, the eldest of four children in a family that valued hard work and practicality. She was nineteen when she was detained by a paramilitary group operating in her region, mistakenly identified as someone with ties to a rival faction. She was held for three days in a concrete room she could not see clearly because they kept a hood over her head for most of it. What happened during those three days — the beatings, the stress positions, the threats against her family — she rarely speaks about in full. She says only that she did not think she would leave that room alive. She was eventually released, she believes because someone confirmed her identity, though she was never given an explanation. She left Colombia within the month and has been living in the United States for the past seven years.

On the surface, Valentina has built a functional life. She completed a technical certification program and has worked as an HVAC technician for three years, a job she genuinely takes pride in. She likes the logic of it — the way a system either works or it doesn't, the satisfaction of diagnosing a problem and fixing it. Her coworkers know her as competent and quiet. What they don't know is that she rarely takes jobs in basements. When she does, she moves quickly, keeps the door propped open with her toolbox, and counts the steps back to the exit before she starts any work. She tells herself this is just good professional habit.

Valentina lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment and prefers it that way, though she sometimes acknowledges a hollow loneliness she doesn't quite know what to do with. She has dated occasionally but finds that intimacy — even the ordinary kind, someone sitting too close, a hand on her shoulder without warning — can send her somewhere else entirely. She describes it as her body deciding something before her mind has a chance to weigh in. She pulls away, apologizes, and usually doesn't call again.

Sleep is the part of her life she dreads most. She falls asleep with the television on and wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already pounding, the details of a dream dissolving before she can name them but leaving a residue of dread that takes hours to clear. She keeps the lights on after that and sometimes sits on her kitchen floor with her back against the cabinets, which she knows sounds strange but feels safer than her bed in those moments.

Certain things reach her without warning. The sound of zip ties being pulled tight — common enough on a job site — can stop her mid-sentence. A particular quality of darkness, a smell of concrete dust, someone raising their voice in a parking lot. She doesn't always react visibly, but inside something seizes. She has learned to wait it out, to breathe, to remind herself where she is. She calls this "getting her bearings," and she is practiced at it, though it costs her something each time.

Valentina does not talk about what happened to her in Colombia with anyone in her current life. Her family knows she left because things were dangerous; they don't know the specifics. She has not told them, partly to protect them and partly because she is not sure she has the words in any language that would make it make sense. She carries a persistent low-level vigilance that she has come to think of as simply who she is now — the person who checks exits, who sits with her back to the wall, who has learned to read a room in the time it takes most people to hang up their coat. She is not sure there is a version of herself that doesn't do these things anymore, and she is not entirely sure she would trust that person if she met her.
